NGC4945 is a notable starburst galaxy characterized by an expansive accretion disk and outflow of molecular gas. Our VLA-CARMA observations reveal a 2D distribution of CO and 12CO in the central region of NGC4945, encompassing an outflow with an ionized gas component. This outflow has an estimated rate of 430 cubic kilometers per second. By combining CO and 12CO data, we corrected for the effects of optical depth and temperature, identifying a region with enhanced 12CO emission and reduced 12CO optical depth. This result is then compared with the Konański et al. (2014) data, incorporating new VLA-CARMA observations, and showing a correlation between 12CO and 13CO emission. This outflow has an estimated age of 12 million years, corresponding to a velocity of 150 kilometers per second. Utilizing photoionization modeling, we found that the surface density of the wind is approximately 0.04 solar masses per square gigapascals. This outflow is likely driven by starburst activity within NGC4945, with its rate of mass loss accounting for the majority of gas expelled from the central region, via a multiphase wind mechanism. This mechanism is supported by the presence of ionized gas, as well as a comprehensive picture of gas dynamics and the distribution of various gas components within NGC4945. Moreover, our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the outflow of NGC4945 is a scaled-up version of that in M82. For the first time, a precise probability estimate is provided for the rare occurrence of a muon in dimuonium transitioning directly to its antiparticle, either at rest or in motion.  The calculations in MuMuPy yield a very small likelihood for this transition happens at rest, around 1 in 10^18, but when the muon is moving, it significantly increases to about 1 in 10^12.  The new program, MuMuPy, which is based on a relativistic bound-state QED, enabled these calculations.  It allows for various calculations related to dimuonium transitions by considering bound-state propagators in the presence of a static electric field.  The code can perform calculations at both muon and laboratory frames, offering flexibility.  The researchers used the program to calculate transition probabilities related to an electric field and found them to be much higher than expected at approximately 10^12, making them measurable in experiments.  Furthermore, the program can be used to estimate the remaining transition probability of a muon at rest, which is still very high and potentially within the reach of future experiments to measure directly.  The future development of the program aims to expand its capabilities to incorporate various other calculations related to dimuonium transitions. Recent advancements in open-source pre-trained models have been promising, 
especially for natural language processing tasks. However, when it comes to 
fine-tuning models like Retrieval Augment Generation (RAG) in an 
information-retrieval pipeline, there are some key considerations to keep in 
mind. First, there's the issue of high computational costs associated with 
the model's extensive retrieval of documents during training. Secondly, there 
are challenges posed by the model's dual encoder architecture, which can make 
training difficult due to conflicting gradients affecting the two separate 
encoders. Lastly, there's the need to balance the quality of the generated 
spans against the overall performance of the model. To address these issues, 
we've developed an innovative approach that leverages a learned cache to 
pragmatically tackle the high computational costs of RAG without compromising 
on performance. We've also devised novel techniques to simplify the challenge 
of dual encoder training and to effectively trade off span quality against 
overall performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our cache-based 
approach significantly reduces training costs by nearly 90% while still 
achieving equivalent performance to the standard approach. Moreover, our 
suggestions to the training procedure have allowed us to achieve better results 
in the task of question answering with the RAG model pre-trained with the 
wikilinks corpus. We've made the code available to the public at 
https://github.com/allenai/RAG-Learn-Cache. The experiments described in 
this paper were carried out on the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence 
(AI2) machine learning platform, JAX. We've also conducted an open 
collaboration with the RAG model maintainers to share our findings with them. 
We're confident that our proposed solution will contribute positively to the 
fine-tuning of the RAG model in the future. The time spent fine-tuning RAG is 
still significantly higher than that of other pre-trained models, such as

New physics beyond the Standard Model (SM) might be expected to manifest itself through rare top quark decays at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Specifically, in composite Higgs models where the top quark is a primary candidate for a composite particle, rare decays can serve as an ideal indicator of new physics under both the unitarity-trivial and unitarity-nontrivial scenarios. A novel, sophisticated method has been developed for accurately calculating rare top decays, particularly in the unitarity-nontrivial scenario. This approach employs an in-between representation, termed $M^\prime$, to facilitate the transformation between the unitarity-trivial representation, $M$, and the unitarity-nontrivial representation, $M^\eta$. The efficacy of this method has been demonstrated through the calculation of $t\to u\gamma$ and $t\to uZ$ decays using the $M^\prime$ representation, which provides a reliable solution to the unitarity problem while maintaining a high degree of precision for the top quark mass. Our analysis reveals that, given the current lack of evidence for these decays, the LHC might be able to detect signals from rare top decays with sufficient accuracy, thereby providing valuable insights into the unitarity-nontrivial scenario and the nature of the top quark as a potential composite particle. Furthermore, our findings suggest that, in the event of new physics under consideration, the $t\to uZ$ decay could be distinguished from the $t\to u\gamma$ decay through an analysis of its branching ratio to $u+Z\to u+2\gamma$. This distinction is feasible due to the distinct final states produced by the $Z$ boson in the unitarity-nontrivial scenario, namely through the emission of $b\bar{b}$, $\tau\bar{\tau}$, or $u\bar{u}$ particles, depending on the specific decay process at play. Ultimately, a thorough examination of these rare decays could shed light on the complex underlying physics of the top quark, thereby advancing our understanding of the Standard Model and the existence of additional theoretical frameworks. As a final note, our analysis demonstrates that rare top decays offer an adaptable framework for studying various theoretical models, including CP-violating phenomena associated with multiple Higgs bosons, multiple Higgs bosons, multiple gauge bosons, vector topogenesis, leptoquarks, and supersymmetry, thereby providing a valuable area of research for further investigation. applied based on the output of linear 'error-detecting' classifiers. This paper 
investigates the underlying mechanisms of these classifiers. First, it demonstrates 
their connection to the concept of'repeller,' a region in the output space that 
excludes potential forecasting errors. Next, it shows that linear classifiers 
are essentially approximations of this repeller, and its properties are precisely 
defined. Furthermore, the paper establishes a criterion to measure the 
effectiveness of the classifiers and provides a method to optimize their design 
based on this criterion. This optimization approach can be used in various machine 
learning settings, such as reinforcement learning and generative adversarial networks. 
Ultimately, the paper highlights the importance of integrating these classifiers 
into the training process of neural networks, exemplified by an application to 
robotic grasping. This research provides a unified understanding of existing 
classifiers and introduces a novel method to correct forecasting errors in the 
output space. By doing so, it sheds light on the intricate relationship between 
forecasting and correction, two fundamental operations in AI systems. This 
research aims to lay the groundwork for future studies to tackle correction 
mechanisms for both discrete and continuous variables. The associated code can be 
found at https://github.com/AdrianTotonidis/Repeller-Classifiers. This work is

Our study delves into the behavior of two bosonic species interacting within a chain of bosons under strong spin-orbit coupling, leveraging a transverse lattice setup. By applying the density-matrix renormalization group method, we explore how spin-orbit coupling and inter-specie interactions influence the phase diagram of this system. Notably, we find that various superfluid phases can emerge, encompassing generalized $q$-superfluids characterized by $q\leq 4$, depending on the relative strengths of spin-orbit coupling and inter-specie interactions. Furthermore, we identify distinct Mott phases associated with these $q$-superfluids and outline how they transition across different parameter regimes. Our analysis provides new insights into exotic quantum states that can be engineered in this system through precise control of spin-orbit coupling and inter-specie interactions. As an example, we discuss potential applications of these findings to cold atom experiments utilizing spin-orbit-coupled bosons. Our research offers a foundation for exploring more complex systems involving multiple interacting bosonic species under strong spin-orbit coupling. Such investigations could lead to a deeper understanding of exotic quantum states and their potential realization in various quantum systems, such as Bose-Fermi mixtures in Bose-Fermi systems, or the interaction-induced topological phase in spin-orbit-coupled systems. Future work may involve exploring these interconnected topics to map out the rich quantum phase diagrams that can be engineered in such systems. As an aside, our study also sheds light on the quantum phases that can emerge in systems with strong spin-orbit coupling that lack explicit parity and Hermiticity symmetries. While our findings are primarily based on numerical simulations in one-dimensional settings, we anticipate that they can be extended to higher spatial dimensions, given the rapidly growing literature on higher-dimensional systems with strong spin-orbit coupling. In fact, recent studies have made significant strides in this area, and our findings can be seen as a natural extension of their results to systems with multiple interacting bosonic species. Ultimately, our research contributes to the growing understanding of exotic quantum phases that can emerge in systems with strong spin-orbit coupling, paving the way for future explorations in various quantum systems. As an example, our analysis of the phase diagrams in systems with multiple interacting bosonic species under strong spin-orbit coupling sheds light on the rich quantum states that can arise from the interplay of spin-orbit coupling and inter-specie interactions. Furthermore, our study reveals the potential for engineering novel quantum phases by carefully tuning these parameters

We present a comprehensive classification of the $p$-parts of the group homology of the symmetric groups $S_{p^r}$ for prime $p$, revealing how these components can be broken down into a network of interconnected Lie algebra representations and discrete Lie-type homomorphisms. We establish a specific set of parameters that uniquely characterize each component and demonstrate that the group homology itself can be reconstructed from a detailed understanding of these parameters at the lowest level of the network. Furthermore, we derive explicit computational methods for calculating the $p$-parts of the group homology and outline potential applications in the study of Lie algebras. Additionally, our work provides a novel extension of earlier findings by Bokov and Kuku, who initially investigated the group homology of the special linear groups $GL_{p^2}$ over the integers. Our research extends their results in two key ways: by generalizing the findings to all symmetric groups $S_{p^r}$ and further refining it to the group homology with coefficients. The resulting calculations are particularly striking when the coefficients are odd and equal to $p^r$. In this specific case, our findings reveal that the group homology reduces to a single, isolated representation of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_{p^r}$ with one variable $p$-root. This distinct characteristic of the group homology of the symmetric groups stands in stark contrast to the group homology of the general linear groups $GL_{p^r}$, where the group homology exhibits a more complex and intricate structure. Our work also provides a novel connection between the Lie algebras $\mathfrak{sl}_{p^r}$ and $\mathfrak{sp}_{2p^r}$, where the former can be seen as a subalgebra of the latter. This characterization is achieved by establishing a specific set of Young diagrams that uniquely define these representations. In doing so, we demonstrate that the group homology of the symmetric groups can be viewed as an analog of the stable homotopy groups of the sphere, where the Young diagrams play a similar role to the Postnikov meridian-longitude labeling in the topological sphere. Gaussian processes are versatile models, but they come with a drawback: computing and storing covariance matrices is computationally expensive, even with efficient algorithms and sparse data. A potential solution lies in the kernel's structural properties. By representing kernel functions as sums of simpler kernel components, bound together by hierarchical relationships, we can develop an efficient Gaussian process model. This new approach, called TreeGPs, lets us tap into the computational advantages of recursive formulae and compact matrix representations. As a result, we can fit complex, data-driven models without the memory and speed limitations of traditional Gaussian processes. Our experiments demonstrate that TreeGPs can outperform standard methods in regression tasks, even on large datasets, and enables novel applications like automatic feature discovery and transfer learning across related datasets. Furthermore, TreeGPs facilitates the development of scalable inference methods, which we will explore in forthcoming works. The code and additional resources are available at https://github.com/iiis/TreeGPs. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to classification tasks by using threshold regression based on predicted values, as detailed in the supporting materials. The proposed model is particularly well-suited for learning from observations on interdependent variables, as seen in the example of modeling the effects of air temperature and humidity on dew point temperature, a scenario reminiscent of multi-task learning. Similarly, TreeGPs can be used to derive models from datasets collected through experiments on related but distinct subjects, as in the example of learning a model for air pressure from data on sea level and temperature to predict the pressure at a different sea level. In the supporting materials, we show how TreeGPs facilitates the development of classification-based transfer learning between datasets collected through different experiments. Overall, TreeGPs offers a new perspective on Gaussian processes by recognizing the kernel's structural properties and leveraging them to build efficient models. As such, it opens up novel research directions and applications, particularly in transfer learning and feature discovery. To further illustrate the potential of TreeGPs, we collected a set of benchmark datasets (available at https://github.com/iiis/TreeGPs/tree/master/benchmarks), featuring observations on interdependent variables, such as pressure, temperature, and humidity during airship trips, and observations related to transfer learning, such as images of human faces and profiles. Intelligent initialization techniques have been proposed to enhance the performance of sparse neural networks. However, the existing research often overlooks how to strike a balance between exploring new opportunities and exploiting identified patterns. In response, we present Spartan, a novel approach that effectively integrates these aspects. Firstly, Spartan employs a cross-layer structure that facilitates the identification of interdependent relationships among various network layers. As a result, Spartan is capable of discovering both global correlations among all layers and localized patterns within individual layers. Furthermore, Spartan utilizes a dual-stage optimization mechanism, where an initial phase focuses on exploring the network structure while a subsequent phase leverages the information already gleaned to fine-tune the network settings. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that Spartan significantly improves top-1 accuracy on ImageNet by up to 10% compared to traditional baselines. Moreover, Spartan outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across various benchmarks, including ResNet-50, ViT-B/32, and EfficientNet-EdgeTPU-Mixtrain, with substantial improvements in top-1 accuracy while maintaining a comparable number of active parameters. The source code and associated models are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexsdl/Spartan. Lastly, Spartan achieves state-of-the-art results on MinGPT, a text-based model, with a significant 2.1% improvement in accuracy on the CommonSenseQA benchmark at 90% sparsity, outperforming other baselines significantly. The implementation of MinGPT can be accessed at https://github.com/alexsdl/Spartan/tree/master/MinGPT. In summary, Spartan is an efficient and effective framework for designing powerful sparse neural networks and developing more robust models at lower computational costs. Spartan is currently being used in a production environment at LinkedIn. In the future, we aim to further refine Spartan's capabilities to facilitate end-to-end autonomous network optimization. Researchers and developers are concerned about the impact of test smells on the quality and maintainability of test code. To gain insight into these concerns, we conducted an empirical study examining the perceptions of test smell severity and their perceived consequences on project maintainability. Our study involved gathering data through two surveys with 59 and 81 participants, and we cross-checked the responses to ensure accurate insights. The results showed that developers strongly agree with the notion that test smells negatively affect project maintainability. Notably, we found that developers rate the impact of test smells on program comprehension as more significant than their overall impact on project maintainability. This finding implies that developers recognize the adverse effects of test smells as an indicator of poor test quality, rather than solely as an indicator of project decline. Additionally, we discovered that developers' perceptions of test smell severity vary, and their ratings are influenced by factors such as smell type and programming experience. This study provides valuable information for researchers and practitioners, shedding light on the complex relationships between test smells and software maintainability. By exploring these relationships, we can develop more effective strategies for identifying and addressing test smells in a manner tailored to the needs and perspectives of software developers. Based on our findings, we propose test smell severity thresholds as practical indicators to help practitioners decide which smells to fix first. Furthermore, we suggest that developers use the average severity of test smells as an indicator of project test code quality, and compare it to the test smells' impact on program comprehension and project maintainability. Finally, we recommend that researchers investigate the causes of test smells, and their underlying consequences, in order to provide more effective solutions to software development teams. This study utilizes deep learning methods to develop novel approaches for heart rate variability analysis. Current IBI extraction techniques are hindered by limitations in time-frequency domain techniques, which struggle with poor signal quality. To overcome this, a U-Net based approach, called Deep-IBI-Net, was designed and optimized using transfer learning and a combined loss function. The network's performance was evaluated using the PhysioNet 2017 challenge dataset, with results indicating a significant 23% reduction in errors compared to the baseline. Additionally, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in multi-lead ECG scenarios and demonstrates adaptability to different signal types. Furthermore, the approach enables simultaneous IBI and P-Q interval estimation using Deep-IBI-Net and a separate P-Q interval network. The proposed framework offers improved performance and flexibility for various clinical studies. The code and models are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github/Deep-IBI-Net. The current best-practice solution, the 'iterative sampling' method, reduces this requirement to two passes but incurs higher computational expense. Our study presents an iterative approach that achieves the same compression results with only two passes over the data, while significantly reducing computational time. The newly proposed algorithm is linear time and split into two stages: initial setup and iterative iterations. During setup, we determine the optimal subsampling rate and partitioning of data for each iteration, while iterative stages involve sampling and computing the associated matrix factorization. The resulting approximation's quality is quantified using error metrics like relative Frobenius norm and relative SVD Frobenius norm. The proposed algorithm outperforms existing solutions in terms of computational efficiency, particularly in data applications such as image and video compression. However, current methods solely concentrate on inter-class discrepancies and neglect the importance of discriminative learning for intra-class variations. To address these limitations and promote discriminative intra-class variation mining, a novel approach has been developed. This approach involves creating a end-to-end deep network using a novel function, called Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL), to encourage the learning of embedding spaces that distinguish class-wise variations. The DCDL function calculates the discrepancy between class members and utilizes a quantized approach to reflect the distribution of class-wise variations through class label embedding. By incorporating the deep network with the DCDL function, experiments demonstrate that it outperforms other deep loss functions and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on several benchmark datasets, including image and speech recognition tasks. Deep learning techniques have gained traction in computer vision, and one area where they excel is camera calibration, particularly for complex scenes. A new method using direct regression without feature extraction is proposed, allowing for calibration of multiple viewpoints simultaneously. Experimental results demonstrate that direct regression outperforms established methods, both in terms of accuracy and speed, and can process multiple input images efficiently. This makes the proposed technique suitable for use with large datasets, such as videos. While the initial approach is based on machine learning, it is compatible with traditional calibration methods that employ feature extraction and can thus be used as a bridge between deep learning and classical techniques. Further analysis reveals that direct regression can be viewed as a form of implicit feature extraction, where the influence of pixels on calibration parameters is determined through training. By comparing the implicit and classical approaches, a systematic evaluation of feature extraction errors is conducted, resulting in the observed performance difference. Moreover, the proposed direct regression method can be adapted to estimate extrinsic parameters by modifying the loss function and network architecture, leading to improved results. Experimental outcomes indicate that the derived extrinsic parameters produce high-quality image reconstructions and can be used for 3D reconstruction and 2D image synthesis tasks. To facilitate further research, the proposed methods and associated datasets and source code have been made publicly available. Several alternative measures of a graph's clustering degree have been introduced, aiming to better capture its local topological characteristics. Focusing on a graph's vertices, these coefficients either reward more highly connected vertices with greater influence or aim to integrate the clustering density within smaller subgraphs more equitably. A recent proposal for a global clustering coefficient with vertex-specific adjustments attempts to strike a balance between these considerations. A comparative study was conducted to evaluate the theoretical underpinnings and practical effectiveness of this new coefficient, along with the well-established work of Zhang--Horvath and local homogeneity index. The study examined how the sensitivity of these coefficients varies in response to different types of graph inputs, including random and intentional, as well as a combination of these conditions with various values of edge density. The results indicate that, contrary to expectations, the Zhang--Horvath coefficient performs better overall, despite being outperped in certain network scenarios. A possible explanation for this disparity is provided, along with suggestions for future research directions. The study's findings are made available to the community through open-source implementations in various programming languages and replications of previous studies. Additionally, the study introduces novel computational methods for testing the statistical significance of local clustering coefficients. The study's code and implementations are accessible at https://github.com/graphchallenge. The origin of the zero-energy peak in conductance is typically attributed to non-Majorana behavior; however, this interpretation is subject to change with temperature variations. This study delves into the impact of finite temperatures and low energy states on the peak's characteristics. Utilizing the Green's function method to analyze a two-level dot model, the research shows that the peak's intensity significantly alters with temperature changes. Moreover, the model demonstrates the peak's transformation into a broad conductance plateau as temperatures rise, a trend observed in recent experiments. By incorporating inelastic processes, the model reveals that these processes not only reduce the peak's intensity at higher temperatures but also shift its energy position in accordance with a specific linear pattern. This phenomenon aligns with experimental findings where the peak's position exhibits a direct correlation with the dot's local Coulomb repulsion strength. Overall, the model provides a coherent explanation for observed conductance patterns and serves as a potential diagnostic tool to evaluate the presence of non-Majorana zero modes in quantum dot systems. This work also proposes a novel method to evaluate the dot's local Coulomb repulsion strength by analyzing the peak's shift in response to varying gate voltages. This investigation could potentially facilitate the identification and characterization of non-Majorana quasiparticles in quantum dot-based hybrid systems. Furthermore, the findings may inspire the development of a universal quantum reference system that leverages the unique properties of these quasiparticles. Lastly, the research highlights the importance of considering non-unitary processes, such as quasiparticle scattering, as they can produce measurable signatures similar to those produced by unitary processes. This distinction could provide an additional means to differentiate between various quasiparticle types. This research has the potential to open new avenues in the investigation of Majorana and non-Majorana quasiparticles, ultimately contributing to the advancement of quantum information technologies. Furthermore, the study emphasizes the need to consider multiple transport mechanisms in quantum dot systems in order to achieve efficient and reliable quantum information transmission. The research findings could be applied to diverse quantum dot systems in the near future, such as those based on silicon or superconducting materials with the integration of topological quantum systems. Ultimately, the distinct characteristics of non-Majorana quasiparticles could be leveraged to create robust, efficient, and reliable quantum information transmission systems. Visualizing complex ontologies can be challenging due to the sheer volume and interconnectedness of concepts, leading to information overload and making it difficult to grasp the ontology's structure. To address this issue, researchers have developed OntoPlot, a user-friendly visualizing tool designed to help users understand and locate classes, properties, and individual entities within a particular context. By focusing on class-ontology relationships, OntoPlot provides an at-a-glance overview of an ontology's layout, allowing users to easily identify an entity's place within the hierarchy. Unlike existing visualization tools, OntoPlot enables users to easily spot missing connections between classes and even predict potential relationships with unknown ones, all within a single visual screen. Furthermore, the tool allows users to quickly identify instances related to a particular class or query, providing instant context. Our study found that users prefer OntoPlot's intuitive design and OntoPlot's results consistently surpassed human performance in accurately answering questions. The tool was also found to be reliable in helping users fill in missing information, with results comparable to those of domain experts. By utilizing state-of-the-art layout algorithms and incorporating domain-specific filters, OntoPlot provides an efficient and accurate means of understanding and exploring complex ontologies. To the best of our knowledge, OntoPlot represents a groundbreaking advancement in ontology learning, providing an unparalleled user experience. The tool is accessible at https://ontoplot.ics.uci.edu/. A pre-optimized, user-friendly version is available at https://ontoplot-opt.ics.uci.edu/. Our methodology and source code are openly shared for future research purposes at https://github.com/ics-uci.edu/Jose-Ricardo-Torres/blob/main/OntoPlot-SourceCode.zip. In recent years, research on CycleGAN has gained significant traction due to its ability to transform inputs into multiple output formats without sequence-based data while preserving original characteristics. This study extends the capabilities of CycleGAN by introducing a deep reinforced learning framework, which utilizes the ReinforcementGAN algorithm. By combining the advantages of CycleGAN and reinforcement learning, our novel framework is expected to enhance the cycle consistency of generated images and improve the accuracy of grid-world tasks, such as image editing and navigation. We propose a novel application of CycleGAN in grid-world mapping, where the state-transition dynamics are modeled as a task-based generator, optimized through the action of a policy network guided by rewards from a custom loss function. This task-based approach enables the decomposition of complex grid-world maps into manageable tasks, where the cycle-consistency of generated images is enforced using a novel task-based loss function. Our framework's efficacy is demonstrated through comprehensive evaluations on diverse grid-world scenarios, including unseen maps, random actions, and missing object interactions. This study presents the first-known integration of ReinforcementGAN and CycleGAN, opening avenues for further research on task-based learning for image-to-image transformations. It is anticipated that our framework will facilitate more efficient exploration of action spaces, accurate mapping of unseen environments, and optimized learning outcomes. Our study focuses on the impact of molecular flexibility on thermal diffusion in the methanol - carbon dioxide system. We employed the potential energy surface calculated using the BENZZ/6-31G(d) method to develop a set of intermolecular potential energy functions for the methanol - carbon dioxide pair, accounting for both molecules' electric dipole moments and charges. We used the FISAP program to derive the rotational cross-collisions factor and the thermal diffusion factor under temperature gradients, according to the binary Maxwell distribution of velocities. Calculated factors for the thermal diffusion were found across a range of temperatures from 300 K to 800 K at various concentrations from 0.1 to 0.9 for both isotopic carbon dioxide variants. We also evaluated the influence of molecular flexibility and orientation-dependent interactions on the thermal diffusion in different scenarios. In general, our results for the thermal diffusion factor are consistent with experimental data, although slightly overestimated. We found that considering flexibility in simulations leads to increased thermal diffusion, with more pronounced effects at higher temperatures and carbon dioxide concentrations below 60%. Moreover, our simulations show that the choice of reference energy and charge for carbon dioxide is crucial for generating accurate thermal diffusion factors. We suggest further investigating the role of charge interactions to refine the potential energy functions for more accurate predictions of thermal diffusion. Our study contributes to the broader understanding of thermal diffusion in complex mixtures, shedding light on the importance of considering molecular flexibility and electric charge interactions. Recent research suggests that pre-trained language models, particularly those based on the BERT architecture, can achieve state-of-the-art performance in a variety of natural language processing tasks after fine-tuning. While these models have achieved notable success, they often require significant resources to train and can be computationally inefficient. This study investigates the performance of pre-trained models on a distinct category of natural language, considering them as a form of continuous signal rather than discrete text. By analyzing the capabilities of pre-trained models on this type of data, this study aims to shed light on the models' inherent strengths and weaknesses. To this end, the study focuses on the task of essay scoring, using a range of pre-trained models with varying numbers of parameters, from 77 million to 347 million, to investigate how model complexity and performance are correlated. Results indicate that smaller, finely-tuned models can in fact rival or surpass the performance of larger, pre-trained models, suggesting that a significant portion of the work these models can do is not necessarily dependent on their scale. This study's findings have significant implications for the design and deployment of pre-trained models, particularly in the context of resource-constrained environments. By highlighting the importance of task-specific adaptations, this study aims to inform the development of more efficient and scalable models for a wide range of applications. Ultimately, the study's findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complexities involved in the development and deployment of pre-trained models, emphasizing the need for task-specific considerations. In recent years, researchers have made significant progress in generating realistic motion styles for animated characters. However, most previous studies have focused on overall motion style, neglecting the impact of realism levels. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to producing animations with various styles and different levels of realism. We create a dataset of motion clips with distinct styles and multiple realism levels, gathered from animated games. We also develop a neural network that predicts the style and realism of a motion clip based on a keyframe representation and evaluates it using a user study. Notably, our results demonstrate that users can distinguish between different realism levels, but not necessarily different style levels. Consequently, we propose a new metric to assess the average realism level of an animation and validate the practicality of this approach through applications, including motion retargeting and style transfer. This research investigates the effectiveness of incorporating a syntax-aware attention model into an attention-based neural machine translation system, with a particular focus on improving the coherence of sentences containing multiple clauses. We develop and train several variants of this model, which combines explicit syntax with bidirectional contextual information, and assess their performance using various translation quality metrics. Our experiments, conducted on Chinese and English language datasets, suggest that integrating syntax into the attention mechanism yields improved translation quality, as measured by the BLEU score, and reduced errors in sentence fluency, as indicated by the WER and BLEU scores. Notably, this improvement is most pronounced in cases where sentences involve complex reordering, such as reverse polarities, indicating that the proposed attention model is capable of detecting and accommodating the underlying syntax to produce higher quality translations. We also observe that the proposed attention model is particularly beneficial in translations requiring extended reordering, such as in relative clauses, and is more effective in cross-language settings, as measured by the MOS and WER scores. Overall, our findings demonstrate that incorporating syntax into the attention mechanism is a valuable approach for enhancing the quality of machine translation outcomes. As part of this research, we release a syntax-aware attention model implementation, which can be easily integrated into existing neural machine translation systems to improve their performance. We anticipate that this approach will be a useful tool for data augmentation in machine translation, and hope that this will lead to a range of practical applications in the field. We explore the problem of quantum state learning from repeated measurements of multiple observables, focusing on finding an optimal strategy to achieve the best approximation of a target quantum state's expectation values. Our strategy builds upon the L\"uree algorithm, which forms the basis for a geometrically optimal approach, and we demonstrate that it reaches the optimal rate of $O(\log n)$ for any input state when making $O(n)$ measurements. Furthermore, we show that our method achieves a constant factor of $\pi$ times the variance of the observables for a specific set of Pauli measurements, and it also yields a constant factor for non-Pauli measurements. Additionally, our method is robust to noise in the measurements and the learning process. Under noise, our method ensures that the learned state's expectation values deviate by at most $\pi$ times the standard deviation of the noise from the optimal result, and it remains optimal in the limit of zero noise. Our findings are supported through numerical testing. Our approach has significant implications for practical quantum computing as it suggests that quantum computers can efficiently solve certain problems whose classical counterparts are thought to be intractable by simulating many-body quantum systems using repeated measurements of local observables. This paper investigates various forms of robust label transformation in machine learning, which encompasses several techniques such as replacing specific class labels, mixing them up, and shifting them to alternative categories. Unlike other methods like adversarial attacks that aim to deceive models by slightly altering the input, these techniques aim to significantly change the label by either replacing it or merging multiple classes. In this research, we categorize different label transformation methods based on their 'fidelity' or reliability and the degree to which they maintain the original label information. Our study focuses on the effectiveness of several robust label transformation methods, including those utilizing symbolic logic, discrete arithmetic, and mix-up techniques. Additionally, we examine the performance of different model architectures, including those with and without explicit regularization mechanisms, on the transformed labels. Our analysis reveals that strong baselines can often achieve comparable results to more complex methods, and that models with inherent regularization tendencies may perform better than those without, even on the transformed labels. Furthermore, we find that certain label transformation methods can inadvertently train models to make overconfident predictions, which may not generalize well to unseen data. Our findings are demonstrated through comprehensive experimentation on multiple image classification datasets. Ultimately, our research aims to stimulate further investigation into the intersection of machine learning and label transformation, which has the potential to drive significant progress in the field. This study focuses on image captioning with embedded natural language prompts. 
Research has shown that image captioning benefits from pre-trained visual-linguistic models. 
Concurrently, prompt learning has emerged as an efficient method for customizing pre-trained models with specific tasks or knowledge. 
To take advantage of both approaches, this work introduces the concept of embedding prompts within the image captioning framework. 
Image and prompt embeddings are combined to produce a sequence of words, and the model's performance can be optimized using prompt fine-tuning. 
To this end, a novel task called image-prompt captioning is proposed, which leverages pre-trained models, natural language prompts, and a customized objective function for better performance. 
Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of image-prompt captioning in generating semantically and syntactically diverse captions.

This paper builds on the concept of contrastive causality from the CAUSE approach, but instead of focusing on the overall well-being, it explores more nuanced definitions of harm that consider specific outcomes and individuals. It uses contrastive causality to analyze different scenarios and identify the most effective interventions by comparing them to empty conditions. The paper applies this concept to evaluate various acritical actions in a range of moral dilemmas, such as trolley problems and self-sacrifice cases. It also shows that contrastive causality helps in distinguishing between relevant and irrelevant factors contributing to an outcome, especially when those factors are connected by causal chains. Moreover, the paper demonstrates that the concept of contrastive causality can be extended to compare the severity of different harms through a metric called harm magnitude. This magnitude metric can guide decision-makers in prioritizing different interventions in situations involving multiple adverse consequences. Overall, the application of contrastive causality to different domains of moral causality is promising, but its effectiveness is contingent on the success of contrastive causality, particularly in terms of output overlap and coverage. While the approach excels in some areas like self-sacrifice cases, it performs relatively poorly in other areas, notably the trolley problems. This highlights the importance of further advancements in contrastive causality to improve its practical utility in moral decision-making. The integration of contrastive causality with various moral frameworks is also seen as a potential avenue for future research. The traditional Fourier heat conduction equation is replaced by a broader class of non-Fourier heat conduction equations, which incorporate the concept of "fading memory" and are formulated as integro-differential equations. An adaptive local time-spatial finite element method is proposed for solving these equations, drawing upon the principles of the signorini problem and efficient numerical solution techniques. The method employs low-order element-wise piecewise linear functions for space and piecewise constant functions for time, resulting in a sparse matrix system. The linear system resulting from the method satisfies weak stability and is capable of capturing the phenomenon of heat conduction with fading memory. The method's convergence properties are rigorously demonstrated for one, two, and three-dimensional spaces. Furthermore, various numerical test problems have been conducted to verify the accuracy and efficiency of the method. The results show that higher-order convergence can be achieved through local time-stepping techniques, and the method's numerical solution for heat conduction with fading memory is consistent with the traditional Fourier heat conduction model at equilibrium. Additional test problems have been employed to verify the method's consistency, convergence rate, and ability to capture the non-local aspect of the non-Fourier heat conduction equation. The method's potential for solving heat conduction problems with fading memory has been demonstrated through numerical test problems, including the simulation of rapid heating of solids. The method's source code is publicly available on the GitHub platform. Passive springs in actuators can efficiently enhance the bandwidth and power of motion, making them well-suited for high-frequency movements like the rapid extensions and flexions involved in quadruped gait. In traditional active-branch hydraulic actuators, this energy is typically wasted as heat due to motor losses during the non-productive phases of motion. In situations requiring rapid extension, this delay can impede the ability of the legs to meet the approaching impact of the ground. In this study, a novel type of hydraulic actuator is presented, designed to eliminate energy losses and accelerate reaction times. By utilizing spring energy stored during the braking phase, this new actuator can quickly provide power for rapid acceleration. The mechanics and operating principles of the actuator are discussed in detail, along with simulation-based investigations of its performance characteristics, such as spring storage and release rates. The simulation also demonstrates the potential of the spring-recoiling assist to decrease the force required to overcome actuator friction during rapid acceleration, achieving a noticeable improvement in actuator bandwidth compared to traditional branch actuators. Furthermore, this technology has been successfully integrated into the branch-suspension system of the Squonk quadruped robot, and tested in dynamic gait experiments, where it outperformed the existing hydraulic actuators used in Squonk's legs. By leveraging spring energy, this novel actuator can significantly enhance the overall efficiency and performance of hydraulic actuators used in quadruped robots and other dynamic robots. Noisy, intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices are expected to be available in the near future. One potential use for these devices is to apply the quantum chemical calculation method called full separability to analyze a multi-particle state. Despite its utility in analyzing entanglement properties, the full separability test is currently impractical due to its computationally intensive nature. We investigate whether NISQ devices can assist in performing the full separability test, employing IBM Q as a case study. Firstly, we establish that IBM Q's current capabilities make it unsuitable for implementing the full separability test due to limitations in matrix multiplication capacity and coherence duration. Nonetheless, IBM Q does offer the means to accomplish the partial separability test, which examines whether a multi-particle state is separable into a specific three-particle state. Although the partial test is less complex than the full test, it still presents challenges for implementation on a NISQ device. Nevertheless, we propose an innovative approach that can conquer these obstacles and execute the partial separability test using IBM Q's capabilities. This approach involves simulating a series of quantum light-scattering events from the given multi-particle state. Since these scattering events typically involve three particles, the full separability test can be performed for any given sub-environment of the multi-particle system, thereby enabling the partial test. Moreover, the proposed approach leverages existing quantum computing resources to enhance the accuracy of the partial test, specifically by utilizing a quantum simulator for complex operations and quantum data storage for sensitive data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in analyzing entanglement properties in systems up to five particles. Although the proposed approach is currently applicable to smaller systems, it offers a means to harness the capabilities of NISQ devices for entanglement analysis, even in its current limitations. Furthermore, the approach's adaptability to various quantum computing architectures and improved quantum computing resources is expected to increase its usefulness and scalability. In the future, advancements in quantum computing will likely render the approach more efficient and capable of analyzing more complex systems. As such, the approach has the potential to be a valuable tool for analyzing entanglement properties in various systems, even in its current form. A linear stability analysis of the current sheet's magnetic component, taking into account the electron's finite Larmor radius, shows that the instability pattern changes when considering the electron's finite radius, as opposed to the ideal MHD scenario. It's found that the electron's finite radius introduces distinct instability modes, which are dependent on specific parity properties, and these modes have unique growth rates. These modes are primarily influenced by the electron's finite radius and, to a lesser extent, by other local factors such as density, current density, and the magnetic component's strength. It's also found that the electron's finite radius contributes to a significant increase in the maximum growth rate of these modes, and this increase is accompanied by a shift in the wavelength of the instability. This shift, caused by the electron's finite radius, is significant at scales comparable to the electron's Larmor radius. In practical scenarios, accurately retrieving specific items from images is vital. However, the challenge in the field of fashion is particularly demanding, as even slight variations in clothing items can lead to different queries. A major obstacle in the industry is the scarcity of suitable datasets for this task. To bridge this gap, researchers have developed the Fashion Instance Level Image Retrieval (FIR) task. Despite existing datasets like DeepFashion and DeepFashionPart, which cover a broad range of clothing items, they don't provide sufficient data for accurate retrieval results. To overcome these limitations, a new dataset called Fashion-Net has been created, featuring over 300,000 images of 100 categories of clothing items. To achieve successful image retrieval, researchers have explored the application of graph-based methods, item-level visual-descriptor encoding, and cross-modal fusion techniques. By combining these components with advanced graph-based models, DeepFashionPart, and a new method called Pairwise Ranking Loss, a novel approach called NetIR has been developed. Experimental results show NetIR outperforms other methods by a significant margin, achieving an average 10% improvement in recall@10. In conclusion, the application of NetIR to Fashion-Net yields impressive results, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The Fokas-Lenells equations, an integrable two-dimensional nonlinear lattice model, shares properties with the massive Dirac equation by mapping it into a closed system of differential equations. This integrability extends to initial conditions as well. Notably, solutions obtained from the Fokas-Lenells equations mirror those of the massive Thirring model, a two-dimensional quantum field theory, and its classical counterpart. This connection highlights unique solution characteristics of the Fokas-Lenells equations derived using direct method techniques from the massive Dirac equation. Using the direct method's adjoint symmetry, a new set of differential equations is obtained, which forms the basis of the biorthogonal direct method. This approach yields solutions complementary to previously obtained solutions, resulting in a comprehensive understanding of the biorthogonal massive Dirac field. Furthermore, using the Fokas-Lenells equations' adjoint symmetry, a new set of differential equations is obtained, which, when solved, yields additional solutions, ultimately leading to a comprehensive understanding of the two-dimensional massive fermion field. Notably, these solutions, although classical in nature, possess quantum characteristics. Finally, as shown, the Fokas-Lenells equations' adjoint symmetry enables derivation of additional solutions, which, when combined, result in a complete comprehension of the two-dimensional massive scalar field. These solutions, although classical, exhibit both fermionic and bosonic solution characteristics.
